body.text: Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka says that his decision to resign was unrelated to the growing scrutiny his educational credentials, but was instead intended to “safeguard the government’s capacity to function.”

Gibran, the eldest son of former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, on Wednesday confirmed his resignation from office, two years after he was elected in a landslide along with President Prabowo Subianto. The vice president has come under pressure since the Constitutional Court and Supreme Court ruled last month that the high-school equivalency certificate he submitted ahead of the 2024 election was legally invalid.
In a seven-minute video message released on social media yesterday, Gibran denied that his decision was connected to the credentials controversy.

“This decision is a personal one. It has nothing to do with my diploma. I repeat: it’s unrelated to my diploma. I have submitted them to the court,” Gibran said, as per the Jakarta Globe. “Hopefully, issues like this will not arise again. Our democracy needs to be better organized. The government administration must provide more certainty.”
The 39-year-old was not especially clear on the reasons for his resignation, but said that it was not an “admission of incapacity.”

“It’s rather a huge step I must take to safeguard the government’s capacity to function,” he said. “This way, they can move forward with greater composure, cohesion, and focus.” He added, “This isn’t an easy decision, but it is the best decision. The unity and the future of the nation are above everything.”

These remarks can be subject to various interpretations. To begin with, it is hard to buy that the timing of his resignation is unrelated to the growing pressure around the validity of his education credentials. It came a day after at least 120 members of the House of Representatives signed a petition asserting their right to initiate a parliamentary inquiry aimed at Gibran’s impeachment. A House session was scheduled to discuss the topic yesterday, prior to the resignation. It is only natural that if his political fate was already sealed, Gibran would wish to avoid a protracted and politically damaging impeachment process.

In its very vagueness, Gibran’s statement also appears to buttress the widespread assumption that his resignation stems from a fallout between Jokowi and Prabowo and their related networks. After competing against one another for the presidency in 2014 and 2019, the pair formed an alliance ahead of the 2024 presidential election. In exchange for Jokowi’s support, Prabowo appointed Gibran as his vice-presidential running mate, aided by a controversial Constitutional Court ruling that waived the minimum age requirement for the then 36-year-old.

But as with the similar alliance between the Marcos and Duterte clans in the Philippines, the Prabowo-Jokowi pact was likely never more than a partnership of short-term expediency. Over the past year, there have been persistent rumors of a split between the two leaders, a proxy for a long-running rivalry between the military and the Indonesian National Police (Polri), which appears to have reached a breaking point in the past fortnight.

Last week, the Indonesian authorities announced that three senior police officials had been arrested for illegally tapping the phones of Prabowo and other prominent politicians, as well as journalists, civil society organizations, and businesspeople. While the exact goals of the wiretappers remain unclear, among the three arrested were Prabowo’s chief of staff, Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo – an ally of Jokowi who served as chief of Polri until his removal from the post on October 1. The president’s office said that the three were under investigation for possible “treason.”

Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto, Listyo’s replacement as Polri chief, told lawmakers yesterday that the wiretappers had also surveilled “senior government officials, politicians, activists and law enforcement personnel,” according to the Associated Press. He said that the suspects will be charged under Article 258 of Indonesia’s Criminal Code, which prohibits the unlawful interception, recording, diversion, alteration, obstruction or monitoring of nonpublic electronic communications. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Evan Laksmana, a Singapore-based analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told the AP that the arrests had appeared to mark an end to the alliance between the two politicians.

“The majority of Prabowo’s political decision making in the past two years always have some Jokowi overshadowing,” Laksmana told the news agency. “So this is kind of Prabowo finally potentially stepping out of Jokowi’s shadow and maybe even going into open political confrontation.”
Prabowo now has 14 days in which to propose two candidates to take over as vice president. The upper house of parliament will then convene within 60 days to choose their preferred candidate.

Speaking to the press yesterday, the Indonesian leader said that he had “regretfully” accepted Gibran’s resignation, which he recognized was “for the greater good, for the sake of the nation and the people of Indonesia,” Nikkei Asia reported.

“In my view, he has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, taking full responsibility and showing statesmanship,” Prabowo said, adding that the public should remain calm and be on the alert against “efforts to divide our nation [and] stir turbulence.”
